source.text: Κἀγὼ ἐλθὼν πρὸς ὑμᾶς, ἀδελφοί, ἦλθον οὐ καθ’ ὑπεροχὴν λόγου ἢ σοφίας καταγγέλλων ὑμῖν τὸ μαρτύριον τοῦ θεοῦ.

records.literal_gloss: And I, having come to you, brothers, came not according to superiority of word or of wisdom, proclaiming to you the testimony of the God.

en.L: And I, when I came to you, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, did not come with superiority of speech or of wisdom, proclaiming to you the testimony of God.
en.B: For my part, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, when I came to you and announced God's testimony to you, I did not come with impressive speech or superior wisdom.
en.R: It was the same with me, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}. When I came to you, I came to tell you what God has done. But I did not try to impress you with fine speeches or clever ideas.

decisions.choice: and I: Paul's own arrival among them followed the same pattern as God's choice of the Corinthians
alternatives: a simple new start with no link to what goes before
decisions.reason: Κἀγὼ ("and I") ties what Paul now says about himself to 1:26-31: God chose what the world counts foolish and weak, and Paul came to them in the same way. It also takes up 1:17, where he says Christ sent him to preach the gospel not with clever speech.

decisions.choice: fellow believers, women and men
decisions.reason: ἀδελφοί addresses the whole church in Corinth, which included women such as Chloe's household (1:11) and Prisca (16:19; Acts 18:2).

decisions.choice: superiority of speech or wisdom: the polished speaking and clever argument that won an audience's admiration
alternatives: a position of authority over them
decisions.reason: ὑπεροχὴν means rising above, excelling. λόγου here is speaking, the speaker's skill, not "the word" of the gospel. In Greek cities public speakers gathered admirers by style and argument, and some in Corinth were comparing preachers in just this way (1:12; 2 Corinthians 10:10). Paul refused to compete on those terms.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "testimony"
decisions.reason: Some early manuscripts read μυστήριον ("mystery") instead of μαρτύριον ("testimony"); the two words look alike in Greek. "Mystery" would anticipate verse 7, and "testimony" echoes 1:6, "the testimony of Christ". The SBLGNT prints "testimony". Either way Paul means the message he brought them. Reviewers must check the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the testimony of God: the message that bears witness to what God has done in Christ
decisions.reason: The genitive could name the one who testifies or the one testified about. In 1:6 "the testimony of Christ" is the witness about Christ, and verse 2 says what the witness was about: Jesus Christ crucified. The message also comes from God, so the two senses are close.

decisions.choice: {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}
decisions.reason: Paul is addressing the whole church, women and men; the traditional form is the alternative.

decisions.choice: superiority of speech or of wisdom (L); impressive speech or superior wisdom (B); fine speeches or clever ideas (R)
decisions.reason: "Excellency" is archaic. Balanced and Readable say what the phrase describes (m3): speaking meant to impress.

decisions.choice: It was the same with me; what God has done
alternatives: And I; the testimony of God
decisions.reason: Readable spells out the link to 1:26-31 (m1) and what the testimony was about (m5).

source.text: οὐ γὰρ ἔκρινά τι εἰδέναι ἐν ὑμῖν εἰ μὴ Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν καὶ τοῦτον ἐσταυρωμένον·

records.literal_gloss: For not I decided anything to know among you except Jesus Christ and this [one] having been crucified;

en.L: For I decided not to know anything among you except Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, and {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} crucified.
en.B: My decision was this: while I was among you, the only thing I would know was Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, and {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} as the one who was crucified.
en.R: While I was with you, I decided that the only thing I would think and talk about was Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, and how {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} died on the cross.

decisions.choice: a firm decision to know nothing else
alternatives: I did not think it right to know anything
decisions.reason: The negative οὐ stands before the verb ἔκρινά but belongs in sense with what follows: Paul made up his mind that he would know nothing but Christ. γὰρ ("for") gives the reason for verse 1: he came without display because this was his whole message.

decisions.choice: to know: to have as the whole subject of his attention and his preaching
decisions.reason: Paul is not claiming ignorance of other things. "Know" here means what he gave himself to and spoke about while among them.

decisions.choice: and him as the crucified one: Christ precisely in his death on the cross
decisions.reason: τοῦτον ἐσταυρωμένον ("and this one, crucified") singles out the cross. The perfect participle presents Jesus as the one who was crucified and remains the crucified one, even as the risen Lord. Crucifixion was the most shameful of deaths, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles (1:23), yet it was the center of Paul's message.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: My decision was this: ...
decisions.reason: Balanced states the decision first and then its content, so the emphasis on "the only thing" is clear.

decisions.choice: think and talk about; how he died on the cross
decisions.reason: Readable says what "know" means here (m2) and spells out "crucified" for young readers.

source.text: κἀγὼ ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ καὶ ἐν φόβῳ καὶ ἐν τρόμῳ πολλῷ ἐγενόμην πρὸς ὑμᾶς, καὶ ὁ λόγος μου καὶ τὸ κήρυγμά μου οὐκ ἐν πειθοῖ σοφίας ἀλλ’ ἐν ἀποδείξει πνεύματος καὶ δυνάμεως, ἵνα ἡ πίστις ὑμῶν μὴ ᾖ ἐν σοφίᾳ ἀνθρώπων ἀλλ’ ἐν δυνάμει θεοῦ.

records.literal_gloss: And I in weakness and in fear and in trembling much came to be with you, \v 4 and the word of me and the proclamation of me [were] not in persuasion of wisdom but in demonstration of Spirit and of power, \v 5 so that the faith of you not may be in wisdom of men but in power of God.

en.L: And I was with you in weakness and in fear and in much trembling, \v 4 and my word and my proclamation [were] not in [the] persuasion of wisdom but in [the] demonstration of [the] Spirit and of power, \v 5 so that your faith might not be in [the] wisdom of {{gender:people|men}} but in [the] power of God.
en.B: While I was with you, I was weak and afraid, and I trembled greatly. \v 4 My message and my preaching did not depend on wisdom's power to persuade; they were proof given by the Spirit and by power, \v 5 so that your faith would be grounded not in human wisdom but in the power of God.
en.R: When I was with you, I felt weak. I was afraid, and I was shaking all over. \v 4 When I spoke and preached to you, I did not try to win you over with clever arguments. Instead, God's Spirit worked with power, and that proved my message was true. \v 5 This was so that your faith would not depend on human wisdom. It would depend on the power of God.

decisions.choice: weakness: Paul's frailty and unimpressive presence, which may have included illness
decisions.reason: ἀσθενείᾳ can mean bodily sickness or weakness in general. Paul's critics said his bodily presence was weak and his speech of no account (2 Corinthians 10:10), and he once preached in Galatia because of an illness (Galatians 4:13). Here the word describes how he came across, in contrast to the confident display of skilled speakers.

decisions.choice: fear and trembling: deep seriousness and anxiety before a weighty task, not mere stage fright
decisions.reason: The pair is common in the Greek Old Testament (Exodus 15:16; Isaiah 19:16), and Paul uses it for earnest, humble seriousness (2 Corinthians 7:15; Philippians 2:12). In Corinth he also had real reason to be afraid: Acts 18:9-10 tells how the Lord told him in a vision not to be afraid there.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "persuasion of wisdom"
decisions.reason: Manuscripts differ a great deal here. Most add "words" (as in verse 13), and many also "human". The SBLGNT prints the short reading πειθοῖ σοφίας, found in a few early witnesses, in which πειθοῖ is read as the noun "persuasion"; the adjective that the longer readings use is otherwise unknown in Greek. All the readings say that Paul's preaching did not rely on persuasive skill. Reviewers must check the apparatus.

decisions.choice: a demonstration given by the Spirit, working with power
alternatives: a demonstration of Paul's own spirit and strength
decisions.reason: ἀποδείξει was a word of the speakers' schools for a compelling proof that settles an argument. Paul says the proof of his message was not argument but the Spirit at work: people turned to God, and signs and wonders went with his preaching (Romans 15:19; 2 Corinthians 12:12; 1 Thessalonians 1:5). "Spirit and power" go together: the Spirit's powerful working.

decisions.choice: my word and my proclamation: what Paul said and the way he announced it, his whole preaching
decisions.reason: λόγος is the message or speech; κήρυγμά is a herald's announcement, used in 1:21 for the preaching God uses to save. Together they cover all his preaching in Corinth.

decisions.choice: so that: the purpose behind the way the gospel came to them
decisions.reason: ἵνα gives the purpose: faith that rests on God's power cannot be shaken as faith won by clever argument could be. "Faith in" here means faith that has its ground in God's power, not faith whose object is power. The purpose is Paul's, and behind it God's (1:27-29).

decisions.choice: {{gender:people|men}}
decisions.reason: ἀνθρώπων means human beings in general. Literal keeps the noun with the traditional form as the alternative; Balanced and Readable say "human", which needs no setting.

decisions.choice: proof given by the Spirit and by power
alternatives: demonstration of the Spirit and of power
decisions.reason: "Demonstration" in English suggests a display or a protest march; "proof" keeps the sense of the speakers' term (m4).

decisions.choice: God's Spirit worked with power, and that proved my message was true
alternatives: in demonstration of the Spirit and of power
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what the proof was and what it proved (m4).

source.text: Σοφίαν δὲ λαλοῦμεν ἐν τοῖς τελείοις, σοφίαν δὲ οὐ τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου οὐδὲ τῶν ἀρχόντων τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου τῶν καταργουμένων·

records.literal_gloss: Wisdom however we speak among the mature, wisdom however not of the age this nor of the rulers of the age this, the [ones] being brought to nothing;

en.L: Yet we do speak wisdom among the mature, but a wisdom not of this age nor of the rulers of this age, who are being brought to nothing.
en.B: There is a wisdom we speak, all the same, among those who are mature. It is not the wisdom of this present age, nor of its rulers, whose power is already being brought to an end.
en.R: But we do teach wisdom to people who are grown up in their faith. It is not the kind of wisdom people value in this present age. It is not the wisdom of the rulers of this age either, and their power is already coming to an end.

decisions.choice: yet we do speak wisdom: after rejecting the world's wisdom, Paul says the gospel has a wisdom of its own
decisions.reason: Σοφίαν stands first for emphasis, and δὲ marks a turn. Having refused to preach with clever wisdom (1:17-2:5), Paul now says the message of the cross is itself God's wisdom (1:24, 1:30). "We" is Paul and those who preach with him (3:5-9).

decisions.choice: the mature: believers who have grown up in faith
alternatives: the initiated, as in the mystery religions
an inner circle of advanced believers
decisions.reason: τελείοις means full-grown, complete. In 3:1-2 and 14:20 Paul sets it against being infants. He is not describing a separate elite with secret teaching: he expects all the Corinthians to become mature, and blames them for staying infants (3:1-3). He may be taking up a word some in Corinth used of themselves, as he seems to in Philippians 3:15.

decisions.choice: this age: the present world-order, which is passing away
decisions.reason: Jewish thought spoke of "this age" and "the age to come". "This age" is the world as it now is, with its values and powers, which God has begun to replace (1:20; Galatians 1:4).

decisions.choice: the rulers of this age: the human authorities who crucified Jesus, and possibly the spiritual powers behind them
decisions.reason: Verse 8 says these rulers crucified the Lord of glory, which points to the authorities in Jerusalem and Rome: the chief priests, Herod and Pilate (Acts 4:26-28; 13:27). Paul uses the same word for human rulers in Romans 13:3. Some read it as the evil spiritual powers (compare Ephesians 6:12; Colossians 2:15), and Paul may see the two together. The text does not settle this.

decisions.choice: being brought to nothing: their power is already being undone, and God is the one undoing it
alternatives: they will be brought to nothing in the future
decisions.reason: The participle καταργουμένων is present and passive: the process is under way now. In 1:28 Paul uses the same verb of God, who chose what is nothing to bring to nothing what is something.

decisions.choice: being brought to an end (B); coming to an end (R)
decisions.reason: Both levels keep the present process (m5). "Their power" is supplied so that it is clear the rulers' rule is ending.

decisions.choice: people who are grown up in their faith
decisions.reason: Readable says what kind of maturity is meant (m2). "Perfect" would suggest people without fault.

source.text: ἀλλὰ λαλοῦμεν θεοῦ σοφίαν ἐν μυστηρίῳ, τὴν ἀποκεκρυμμένην, ἣν προώρισεν ὁ θεὸς πρὸ τῶν αἰώνων εἰς δόξαν ἡμῶν·

records.literal_gloss: but we speak of God wisdom in mystery, the [wisdom] having been hidden, which foreordained the God before the ages for glory of us;

en.L: but we speak God's wisdom in a mystery, the [wisdom] that has been hidden, which God foreordained before the ages for our glory.
en.B: Instead, the wisdom we speak is God's own, a mystery that has been kept hidden. God planned it before the ages for our glory.
en.R: We speak about God's wisdom, which used to be a secret. God kept it hidden. But long before the world began, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} planned it so that we would share in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} glory.

decisions.choice: God's wisdom: the word God stands first, in contrast to the wisdom of this age
decisions.reason: θεοῦ comes before σοφίαν for emphasis: the wisdom Paul speaks is not the wisdom "of this age" (verse 6) but God's.

decisions.choice: a mystery: God's wisdom was hidden in the past and is now made known
alternatives: Paul speaks in a secretive way, as to initiates
decisions.reason: For Paul a mystery is not a riddle kept from outsiders but God's plan, hidden through past ages and now revealed (Romans 16:25-26; Colossians 1:26). The phrase describes the wisdom, not a hidden manner of speaking, for verse 10 says God has revealed it.

decisions.choice: planned beforehand, before the ages
decisions.reason: προώρισεν means to decide or mark out in advance. πρὸ τῶν αἰώνων ("before the ages") places God's plan before time and history began. The cross was not an accident or a defeat but the wisdom God had planned.

decisions.choice: for our glory: the share in God's glory that believers are to have
alternatives: for our honor or fame now
decisions.reason: Glory here is the splendor of God's presence that believers will share when Christ comes (Romans 8:18, 8:30; 2 Corinthians 4:17). It contrasts with the rulers whose power is passing (verse 6), and points to "the Lord of glory" in verse 8.

decisions.choice: mystery (L, B); secret (R)
decisions.reason: As in Colossians 1:26-27: "mystery" is the term Paul uses, and Readable says "secret", since "mystery" can suggest something that can never be understood.

decisions.choice: used to be a secret; share in his glory
alternatives: that has been hidden; for our glory
decisions.reason: Readable says that the secret is now told (m2) and what "our glory" means (m4).

source.text: ἣν οὐδεὶς τῶν ἀρχόντων τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου ἔγνωκεν, εἰ γὰρ ἔγνωσαν, οὐκ ἂν τὸν κύριον τῆς δόξης ἐσταύρωσαν·

records.literal_gloss: which none of the rulers of the age this has known, for if they had known, not [would] the Lord of the glory they have crucified;

en.L: which none of the rulers of this age has understood; for if they had understood [it], they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.
en.B: Not one of this age's rulers grasped this wisdom. Had they grasped it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.
en.R: None of the rulers of this present age understood God's wisdom. If they had, they would not have killed the glorious Lord on a cross.

decisions.choice: which: God's wisdom (verse 7)
decisions.reason: ἣν picks up the wisdom of verse 7, as the relative in that verse did. The rulers failed to understand God's plan.

decisions.choice: an unreal condition: they did not understand, and so they crucified him
decisions.reason: εἰ with the past tense and ἂν states something contrary to fact. Their crucifying Jesus shows that they did not understand; in their ignorance they carried out the very plan God had made (Acts 3:17-18).

decisions.choice: the Lord of glory: the Lord to whom glory belongs, a title used of God
alternatives: a glorious lord, as an earthly ruler might be called
decisions.reason: In the Psalms God is "the King of glory" (Psalm 24:7-10) and "the God of glory" (Psalm 29:3; compare Acts 7:2). Paul gives this kind of title to the crucified Jesus (compare James 2:1). The one put to the most shameful of deaths is the Lord who has God's glory.

decisions.choice: killed on a cross
decisions.reason: Readable says what crucifying meant, as in verse 2.

decisions.choice: the glorious Lord
decisions.reason: Readable turns the Hebrew-style phrase into a plain adjective; the key term is kept (m3).

source.text: ἀλλὰ καθὼς γέγραπται· Ἃ ὀφθαλμὸς οὐκ εἶδεν καὶ οὖς οὐκ ἤκουσεν καὶ ἐπὶ καρδίαν ἀνθρώπου οὐκ ἀνέβη, ὅσα ἡτοίμασεν ὁ θεὸς τοῖς ἀγαπῶσιν αὐτόν.

records.literal_gloss: but just as it has been written: What eye not saw and ear not heard and upon heart of man not came up, as many as prepared the God for those loving him.

en.L: But, just as it is written, "Things that eye has not seen and ear has not heard, and [that] have not come up upon [the] heart of {{gender:a human being|man}}, all that God has prepared for those who love {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}."
en.B: But this is what Scripture describes: "Things no eye ever saw and no ear ever heard, things that never rose up in any human heart: these God has made ready for those who love {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}."
en.R: But this is what the Scriptures say: "Nobody has ever seen it or heard of it. Nobody has ever even dreamed of it. That is what God has made ready for the people who love {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}."

decisions.choice: a quotation drawn mainly from Isaiah 64:4
alternatives: a quotation from a book now lost
decisions.reason: No known text has these exact words. They are closest to Isaiah 64:4 (64:3 in the Hebrew and Greek): "from of old no one has heard, no ear has perceived, no eye has seen a God besides you, who acts for those who wait for him". "Come up upon the heart" is a phrase of the Greek Old Testament (compare Isaiah 65:17), and Isaiah 52:15 speaks of kings seeing what they had not been told. The early Christian writer Origen thought Paul was quoting a lost book, the Apocalypse of Elijah. Most likely Paul joins and adapts words from Isaiah. Isaiah says "those who wait for him"; Paul says "those who love him", the language of God's covenant people (Deuteronomy 7:9).

decisions.choice: an unfinished sentence: the quotation sets God's gift against the rulers' ignorance, and verse 10 completes the thought
alternatives: the quotation is the object of "we speak" in verse 7
decisions.reason: ἀλλὰ contrasts with verse 8: the rulers did not understand, but, as Scripture says, God has prepared what no one could have known. The relative clauses of the quotation have no main verb; verse 10 supplies the point: God has revealed these things to us. Some take the quotation as the object of "we speak" in verse 7; the sense is the same.

decisions.choice: come up upon the heart: occur to someone, be imagined
decisions.reason: In biblical language the heart is where a person thinks and plans. Something that has not "come up upon the heart" has never entered anyone's mind.

decisions.choice: what God has prepared: the whole of God's saving wisdom in Christ, revealed now and complete in the future
decisions.reason: The words are often applied to heaven. In context they describe God's wisdom, hidden before and now revealed through the Spirit (verse 10), so they include what believers already know as well as what is still to come.

decisions.choice: Scripture describes (B); the Scriptures say (R)
decisions.reason: "It is written" is the standard formula for quoting Scripture; Balanced and Readable name Scripture. Literal keeps the formula.

decisions.choice: {{gender:a human being|man}}
decisions.reason: ἀνθρώπου means any human being. Balanced says "any human heart" and Readable "nobody", which need no setting.

decisions.choice: three short sentences
alternatives: one long sentence with relative clauses
decisions.reason: Readable breaks the quotation into short sentences and puts the sense of the idioms (m3) in everyday words. It makes a complete sentence of the unfinished quotation (m2).

source.text: ἡμῖν γὰρ ἀπεκάλυψεν ὁ θεὸς διὰ τοῦ πνεύματος, τὸ γὰρ πνεῦμα πάντα ἐραυνᾷ, καὶ τὰ βάθη τοῦ θεοῦ.

records.literal_gloss: To us for revealed the God through the Spirit; the for Spirit all things searches, even the depths of the God.

en.L: For to us God revealed [these things] through the Spirit; for the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God.
en.B: And it is to us that God has made them known, through the Spirit. For nothing is beyond the Spirit's searching, not even the depths of God.
en.R: But God has shown these things to us through {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} Spirit. The Spirit looks into everything, even the deepest things about God.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "for"
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts read "but" instead of γὰρ ("for"). The SBLGNT prints "for", which some early witnesses have. With "for", verse 10 explains how the hidden things of verse 9 are known; with "but", it contrasts us with the rulers of verse 8. The meaning is much the same. Reviewers must check the apparatus.

decisions.choice: to us: emphatic, in contrast to the rulers who did not understand
decisions.reason: ἡμῖν stands first. What the rulers of this age did not know (verse 8), God has made known to believers.

decisions.choice: the Spirit: the Spirit of God, the Holy Spirit
decisions.reason: Verse 11 calls him "the Spirit of God", and verse 12 "the Spirit who is from God".

decisions.choice: searches: knows thoroughly, down to the depths; not hunting for what he does not know
decisions.reason: ἐραυνᾷ means to search or examine. Said of the Spirit, it means complete knowledge of God, even "the depths": God's hidden purposes, which are beyond human tracing (Romans 11:33).

decisions.choice: it is to us that God has made them known
alternatives: God has revealed them to us
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the emphasis on "to us" (m2).

decisions.choice: his Spirit
decisions.reason: Readable says whose Spirit is meant (m3).

source.text: τίς γὰρ οἶδεν ἀνθρώπων τὰ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου εἰ μὴ τὸ πνεῦμα τοῦ ἀνθρώπου τὸ ἐν αὐτῷ;

records.literal_gloss: Who for knows of men the things of the man except the spirit of the man the [one] in him?

en.L: For who among {{gender:human beings|men}} knows the things of a {{gender:person|man}} except the spirit of the {{gender:person|man}} that is in {{gender:that person|him}}?
en.B: After all, what human being knows what is going on inside someone else? Only that person's own spirit within knows it.
en.R: Think about it: no one can know what someone else is thinking. Only that person's own spirit, deep inside, knows it.

decisions.choice: a question that expects the answer "no one"
decisions.reason: τίς γὰρ ("for who") opens a question that states a fact everyone knows, as an illustration for what follows.

decisions.choice: the things of a person: their inner thoughts, plans and purposes
decisions.reason: The neuter article with a genitive means "what belongs to" someone: here what is in a person's mind, which no one else can see.

decisions.choice: the spirit of a person: the inner self, aware of its own thoughts
decisions.reason: Paul uses the human spirit as an analogy. Just as only you know what is in your mind, only God's Spirit knows what is in God's. The comparison is about knowing from within; it does not say that God's Spirit relates to God exactly as the human spirit does to a person.

decisions.choice: {{gender:human beings|men}}; {{gender:person|man}}; {{gender:that person|him}}
decisions.reason: ἀνθρώπων and ἀνθρώπου mean human beings in general, men and women alike. Literal keeps the nouns with the traditional forms as the alternative.

decisions.choice: what is going on inside someone (B); what someone is thinking (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "the things of a person" are (m2), and need no gender setting.

source.text: οὕτως καὶ τὰ τοῦ θεοῦ οὐδεὶς ἔγνωκεν εἰ μὴ τὸ πνεῦμα τοῦ θεοῦ.

records.literal_gloss: So also the things of the God no one has known except the Spirit of the God.

en.L: So also no one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God.
en.B: In the same way, the things of God are known to no one but the Spirit of God.
en.R: In the same way, only God's Spirit knows what God is thinking.

decisions.choice: has known: has come to know and so knows
decisions.reason: ἔγνωκεν is perfect: knowledge gained and held. Paul uses it as a present, "knows".

decisions.choice: the Spirit knows God from within
decisions.reason: The Spirit knows the things of God as a person's own spirit knows that person's thoughts. So what the Spirit reveals (verse 10) is God's own mind, not a guess about God. The Spirit belongs to God, not to the world (verse 12).

decisions.choice: what God is thinking
decisions.reason: Readable carries over the sense of the comparison in the previous sentence.

source.text: ἡμεῖς δὲ οὐ τὸ πνεῦμα τοῦ κόσμου ἐλάβομεν ἀλλὰ τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ, ἵνα εἰδῶμεν τὰ ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ χαρισθέντα ἡμῖν·

records.literal_gloss: We however not the spirit of the world received but the Spirit the [one] from the God, so that we may know the things by the God having been freely given to us;

en.L: Now we did not receive the spirit of the world but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things freely given to us by God.
en.B: We, for our part, have not received the spirit of the world. We have received the Spirit who comes from God, so that we may recognize all that God has graciously given us.
en.R: We have not been given the spirit that belongs to this world. God has given us {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} own Spirit. Now we can understand all the good things God has freely given us.

decisions.choice: we: all who believe, who received the Spirit when they came to faith
alternatives: Paul and his fellow preachers only
decisions.reason: In verses 6-7 "we speak" is Paul and those who preach with him. Receiving the Spirit is true of every believer (12:13; Galatians 3:2), so "we" here includes the Corinthians too. The aorist ἐλάβομεν points to the time they believed.

decisions.choice: the spirit of the world: the outlook and wisdom of humanity apart from God
alternatives: an evil spirit who rules the world
decisions.reason: The phrase is set against "the Spirit who is from God". κόσμου is the world of human beings turned away from God, whose wisdom did not know God (1:20-21). Paul can speak of a spirit at work in those who disobey (Ephesians 2:2), but here the contrast is mainly between two sources of understanding.

decisions.choice: freely given: gifts of God's grace, all that God gives in Christ
decisions.reason: χαρισθέντα is related to the word for grace. The things "freely given" are what God has prepared for those who love him (verse 9): salvation and everything that comes with it.

decisions.choice: graciously given
decisions.reason: Balanced brings out the link to grace (m3); Literal and Readable say "freely given".

decisions.choice: God has given us his own Spirit
alternatives: the Spirit who is from God
decisions.reason: Readable names the giver and says plainly that the Spirit is God's.

source.text: ἃ καὶ λαλοῦμεν οὐκ ἐν διδακτοῖς ἀνθρωπίνης σοφίας λόγοις, ἀλλ’ ἐν διδακτοῖς πνεύματος, πνευματικοῖς πνευματικὰ συγκρίνοντες.

records.literal_gloss: which also we speak not in taught of human wisdom words but in [those] taught of Spirit, to spiritual [things] spiritual things interpreting.

en.L: These things we also speak, not in words taught by human wisdom but in [words] taught by [the] Spirit, interpreting spiritual things with spiritual [words].
en.B: When we speak of these things, our words are not lessons learned from human wisdom. The Spirit teaches them, and so we explain spiritual things in words the Spirit gives.
en.R: That is what we talk about. We do not use words that human wisdom has taught us. We use words that the Spirit has taught us. So we use the Spirit's words to explain the things that come from the Spirit.

decisions.choice: which we also speak: the gifts God has given (verse 12) are also what Paul preaches
decisions.reason: ἃ looks back to "the things freely given" in verse 12. Having received and understood them by the Spirit, Paul also speaks them.

decisions.choice: words taught by human wisdom, and words taught by the Spirit
decisions.reason: διδακτοῖς means "taught", and the genitives name the teacher: human wisdom in one case, the Spirit in the other. Paul is not saying the words fall from heaven; he is saying where his message and its way of speaking come from.

decisions.choice: spiritual things in spiritual words
alternatives: spiritual things with other spiritual things
decisions.reason: πνευματικοῖς can be neuter, "spiritual [words or things]", or masculine, "spiritual [people]". The neuter fits the sentence, which is about words; the masculine fits verses 14-15, which turn to the spiritual person. The difference is small: either way the Spirit gives both the message and the understanding.

decisions.choice: interpreting, explaining
decisions.reason: συγκρίνοντες usually means to combine or to compare (as in 2 Corinthians 10:12). In the Greek Old Testament it is used for interpreting dreams (Genesis 40-41), and that sense suits a sentence about how the gifts of God are put into words.

decisions.choice: the words are described in a sentence of their own
alternatives: in words not taught by human wisdom but taught by the Spirit
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable unpack the compact Greek phrase into separate statements, so that it is clear who teaches the words (m2).

decisions.choice: spiritual things in words the Spirit gives (B); the Spirit's words to explain the things that come from the Spirit (R)
alternatives: interpreting spiritual things to spiritual people
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable follow the reading chosen in m3 and say that "spiritual" means from the Spirit; the footnote gives the other reading.

source.text: Ψυχικὸς δὲ ἄνθρωπος οὐ δέχεται τὰ τοῦ πνεύματος τοῦ θεοῦ, μωρία γὰρ αὐτῷ ἐστίν, καὶ οὐ δύναται γνῶναι, ὅτι πνευματικῶς ἀνακρίνεται·

records.literal_gloss: Natural however man not accepts the things of the Spirit of the God, foolishness for to him it is, and not he is able to know, because spiritually it is examined;

en.L: But [the] {{gender:natural person|natural man}} does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to {{gender:that person|him}}, and {{gender:that person is|he is}} not able to know [them], because they are examined spiritually.
en.B: A person who has only natural life does not welcome what belongs to the Spirit of God. It all seems foolish to such a person, who cannot grasp it, because it can be weighed rightly only by the Spirit.
en.R: People who do not have God's Spirit will not accept the things that come from the Spirit. They think these things are foolish. They cannot understand them, because only the Spirit can help people see what these things really mean.

decisions.choice: a natural person: someone who has only ordinary human life, without the Spirit of God
alternatives: a person ruled by the senses
the soul as a lower part of a person
decisions.reason: Ψυχικὸς comes from ψυχή, "life, soul": it describes life as people have it by nature. Paul sets it against πνευματικὸς ("spiritual") here and in 15:44-46, where the natural body is set against the spiritual body. Jude 19 describes people as natural, "not having the Spirit". Paul is not dividing a person into soul and spirit; he contrasts life without God's Spirit and life with it.

decisions.choice: does not accept: refuses to welcome as true
decisions.reason: δέχεται means to receive or welcome, as a guest or a message (1 Thessalonians 1:6; 2:13). Such a person hears but does not welcome the message.

decisions.choice: foolishness: the same verdict the world passes on the message of the cross
decisions.reason: μωρία takes up 1:18 and 1:23, where the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing.

decisions.choice: examined spiritually: weighed and judged rightly only with the Spirit's help
decisions.reason: ἀνακρίνω means to examine or question closely, as a judge does at a hearing (Acts 4:9). It recurs in verse 15 and in 4:3-4, where Paul refuses to be judged by the Corinthians. πνευματικῶς ("spiritually") means by means of the Spirit.

decisions.choice: {{gender:natural person|natural man}}; {{gender:that person|him}}; {{gender:that person is|he is}}
decisions.reason: ἄνθρωπος means a human being, man or woman. Literal keeps the singular with the traditional forms as the alternative; Balanced says "person" and Readable "people", which need no setting.

decisions.choice: a person who has only natural life (B); people who do not have God's Spirit (R)
decisions.reason: "Natural" alone suggests something healthy or unprocessed, and "soulish" is not English. Balanced keeps the idea of natural life; Readable says what is missing (m1).

source.text: ὁ δὲ πνευματικὸς ἀνακρίνει τὰ πάντα, αὐτὸς δὲ ὑπ’ οὐδενὸς ἀνακρίνεται.

records.literal_gloss: The however spiritual [one] examines all things, he however by no one is examined.

en.L: But the spiritual [person] examines all things, but {{gender:that person|he himself}} is examined by no one.
en.B: But the spiritual person is able to assess all things, while no one is in a position to assess such a person.
en.R: But people who have the Spirit can judge what is true about everything. And no one without the Spirit is able to judge them.

decisions.choice: the spiritual person: one who has God's Spirit and is guided by the Spirit
alternatives: a person with unusual spiritual experiences
decisions.reason: πνευματικὸς is the opposite of the natural person in verse 14. In 3:1 Paul says he could not speak to the Corinthians as spiritual people, though they had the Spirit, because they lived by merely human standards: being spiritual shows in how one lives.

decisions.choice: examines all things: can weigh rightly everything that concerns God's gifts and God's ways
decisions.reason: ἀνακρίνει is the verb of verse 14. Paul does not claim that spiritual people know everything; he means that the Spirit enables them to judge rightly the things the natural person cannot (verse 14).

decisions.choice: no one without the Spirit is in a position to pass judgment on a spiritual person
alternatives: spiritual people are answerable to no one at all
decisions.reason: Paul does not put spiritual people beyond correction: he corrects the Corinthians at length, and prophecy is to be weighed (14:29). The point is that a natural person cannot judge the things of the Spirit or those who live by them. In 4:3-4 Paul applies this to the Corinthians' judging of him: the Lord is his judge.

decisions.choice: {{gender:that person|he himself}}
decisions.reason: αὐτὸς refers to the spiritual person, who may be a man or a woman. Balanced says "such a person" and Readable uses the plural, which need no setting.

decisions.choice: no one without the Spirit
decisions.reason: Readable makes explicit who "no one" refers to (m3). This narrows Paul's general statement and is marked for reviewers.

source.text: τίς γὰρ ἔγνω νοῦν κυρίου, ὃς συμβιβάσει αὐτόν;

records.literal_gloss: Who for knew [the] mind of [the] Lord, who will instruct him?

en.L: For "who has known [the] mind of [the] Lord, who will instruct {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}?"
en.B: For "who has ever known the mind of the Lord well enough to instruct {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}?"
en.R: The Scriptures ask, "Who knows what the Lord is thinking? Who can teach {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} anything?"

decisions.choice: a quotation of Isaiah 40:13, in the form of the Greek Old Testament
decisions.reason: Isaiah 40:12-14 asks who could measure the world or teach God anything. Paul quotes the Greek form of verse 13, as he does in Romans 11:34, without an introduction. Where the Greek has "mind", the Hebrew has "spirit": "Who has measured the Spirit of the LORD?" The Hebrew word fits Paul's subject closely.

decisions.choice: Lord: in Isaiah 40:13 this stands for God's own name, the LORD
decisions.reason: In the Hebrew of Isaiah 40:13 the word is the divine name. Here it means God, whose mind no one can know except his Spirit (verse 11). The next sentence then speaks of "the mind of Christ".

decisions.choice: who will instruct him: no one knows the Lord's mind well enough to teach him
decisions.reason: The relative ὃς gives the consequence: who knows God's mind so as to teach him? The expected answer is no one. Verse 15 is not a claim to stand over God.

decisions.choice: Lord
decisions.reason: The style guide keeps "the LORD" for the divine name in the Old Testament itself. Here Paul quotes the verse with the Greek word "Lord"; meaning decision m2 explains whom it means.

decisions.choice: The Scriptures ask
decisions.reason: Paul does not say he is quoting; Readable tells the reader that these words are from Scripture (m1).

records.literal_gloss: We however [the] mind of Christ have.

en.B: But we have the mind of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.
en.R: But we have been given the mind of {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}. Through the Spirit we understand how {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} thinks.

decisions.choice: the mind of Christ: Christ's understanding of God's purposes, his way of thinking, given to believers by the Spirit
alternatives: the mind that thinks like Christ by human effort
decisions.reason: νοῦν is understanding and outlook. Believers do not know everything God knows; they share, through the Spirit (verse 12), Christ's understanding of God's wisdom, the cross included. Compare Philippians 2:5.

decisions.choice: Christ stands where Isaiah has the Lord
decisions.reason: The quotation asked who has known "the mind of the Lord"; Paul answers with "the mind of Christ". He applies to Christ what Isaiah said of the LORD, as he does in 8:6.

decisions.choice: we: those who have received the Spirit from God
decisions.reason: ἡμεῖς is emphatic and takes up "we" of verse 12: by the Spirit, believers have what no natural person has.

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}
decisions.reason: Title setting.

decisions.choice: we have been given; through the Spirit we understand how he thinks
decisions.reason: Readable says how believers have Christ's mind and what it means (m1, m3).
